title: One Indian Seafarer Missing, Two Injured After Hormuz Tanker Attack
excerpt: India condemned the November 16 attack on the LPG tanker MT Tara Gas in the Strait of Hormuz. Twenty-one of the 24 Indians aboard were evacuated to Khasab in Oman, and the search for the missing crew member continues.
body:
• One Indian seafarer is missing and two are in hospital after the Panama-flagged LPG tanker MT Tara Gas was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz on November 16, India's Ministry of External Affairs said on Tuesday.
  • Of the 24 Indian nationals aboard, 21 have been safely evacuated ashore at Khasab in Oman; the Indian Embassy in Oman is monitoring the search and rescue operation with Omani authorities.
  • The toll replaced an earlier all-safe report: after the first strike the crew was reported unhurt, but a subsequent attack forced the entire crew to abandon the vessel, Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal said.
  • It is the second attack in a week on a ship carrying Indian crew in the Gulf: the VLCC MT Fujairah Energy, with six Indian seafarers aboard, was struck on November 10, injuring four crew including one Indian.

India on Tuesday condemned the attack on the Panama-flagged LPG tanker MT Tara Gas in the Strait of Hormuz, confirming that one Indian seafarer is missing, two are injured and in hospital, and 21 have been evacuated to safety in Oman. The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said the vessel, carrying 24 Indian nationals among a crew of 25, was attacked on Monday, November 16, while transiting outbound through the strait.

"We condemn the attack on the Panama-flagged LPG tanker MT TARA GAS in the Strait of Hormuz on 16 November 2026," the MEA said. "Of the 24 Indian nationals on board, 21 have been safely evacuated ashore at Khasab, two injured Indian crew members have been admitted to hospital, while one Indian national remains missing."

How the picture changed within a day

The first reports were reassuring, and they were overtaken by events. After the initial strike, Union Minister for Ports, Shipping and Waterways Sarbananda Sonowal said all 24 Indian nationals and the entire 25-member crew were safe with no injuries, and that the government was in close contact with the ship's management company. Sonowal later disclosed that the tanker was subjected to a subsequent attack, which forced the entire crew to abandon the vessel. "While 24 crew members have been safely accounted for, one Indian seafarer remains missing," he posted on X, adding that authorities were urgently coordinating with the management company and regional rescue authorities to locate him.

The MEA said the Indian Embassy in Oman is closely monitoring the ongoing search and rescue operations in coordination with the Omani authorities, and thanked Oman for its timely assistance and support. The government has not publicly named the missing seafarer, and had not attributed responsibility for the attack to any group as of Tuesday.

"The continuing incidents of attacks on shipping in the region are deeply worrisome and pose a serious threat to the safety of civilian seafarers. The targeting of commercial shipping and civilian infrastructure must end, and free and unimpeded navigation and commerce through international waterways, in keeping with international law, must be restored at the earliest."

— Ministry of External Affairs, India

A second ship in a week

The Tara Gas attack is not an isolated incident for Indian crew in the Gulf. On November 10, the Liberia-flagged very large crude carrier MT Fujairah Energy, carrying six Indian seafarers, was struck by a projectile while transiting the Persian Gulf, leaving four crew members injured, including one Indian national, according to Nation Press's account of the week's incidents.

The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman connecting the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea, is one of the world's most important energy shipping routes: an average of around 20 million barrels of crude oil and oil products passed through it daily in 2025, about a quarter of global seaborne oil trade, according to the IEA figures cited by The Business Standard. The strait has been effectively closed to normal commercial shipping since February 28, 2026, following the outbreak of war involving the United States, Israel and Iran, The Business Standard reported.

What happens next

The search for the missing seafarer continues, with India's embassy in Oman as the coordination point for the rescue effort and for the crew members now ashore at Khasab and in hospital. For the families of Indian seafarers serving on Gulf routes — a workforce drawn from coastal states across India and a mainstay of the world's merchant fleets — the MEA's statement is the authoritative channel: it is updating the crew's status as the search proceeds, and any family seeking information on a crew member of the Tara Gas should go through the embassy in Oman and the ship's management company, the two channels the government says it is working through.
